items.excerpt: Tech developers think automation will fundamentally reshape the work of literary translators, but not everyone is on board. PW talks to translators and AI vendors about what machine-assisted literary translation actually produces.

When claim notices in the $1.5 billion Anthropic agreement went out, many authors were surprised they would not receive what they believed was their share. The Authors Guild walks through how the payouts are split between writers and publishers.

Google launched Expert Intelligence, letting readers use purchased e-books and other vetted sources directly inside its AI products, with more than 100,000 publisher titles at launch — a new licensed route from book to AI answer.

The US government filed in support of AI companies in the copyright suit brought by publishers and authors, arguing AI development should not be restrained by licensing requirements — a direct hit to authors' leverage over training data.
Publishing leaders respond to the DOJ's pro-fair-use filing in NYT v. OpenAI, debating whether a real content-licensing market for AI training can survive if training is ruled fair use.

A guest post argues the journal portfolio, platform and membership bundle no longer holds as AI changes how research is discovered and consumed, and lays out the trilemma publishers face in rebuilding their products.

A new interactive exhibition on James Baldwin's writing features an AI-programmed typewriter that surfaces passages from his books, essays and letters — a test case for AI as literary archive interface rather than text generator.

While publishing frets over AI-written books, readers are prompting chatbots to generate custom fiction built to their own taste — a demand-side shift in storytelling that routes around the industry entirely.

Pangram has become the default AI-detection tool used by publishers, magazines and platforms to decide whose writing is machine-made. WIRED examines how reliable it is and what a false positive costs a writer.
Pocket FM now produces 93% of its audio-series content with AI, cutting production costs roughly 80x — a working industrial model for AI-written, AI-narrated serialized fiction.

A literature undergrad's AI pipeline produced a near-complete Mandarin version of Haruki Murakami's new novel in four hours for about $2, splitting China's literary world over what's left for human translators and rights holders.
As digital checkouts soar, Los Angeles public libraries are retooling around AI education and paywall-bridging services — a shift in how readers are taught to find and evaluate sources.
